ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Neurodevelopmental Disorders II covers ADHD and disruptive behaviour disorders, focusing on clinical presentation, diagnosis, severity grading, causes, investigations and management in diverse settings.

sections.p: ADHD is a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity‑impulsivity that interferes with functioning. Disruptive behaviour disorders (ODD, CD) involve chronic irritability, defiance or violation of rights.
b: DSM‑5 criteria require ≥6 symptoms for >6 months in children, present in two settings, and onset before age 12.
ODD: ≥4 symptoms of angry/irritable mood, argumentative behaviour, or vindictiveness.
CD: ≥3 serious rule‑breaking behaviours (aggression, property destruction, theft, serious rule violations).

t.a: Clinical interview with child and caregivers
t.b: Confirms symptom count, duration, cross‑setting presence; distinguishes ADHD from normal developmental variation.
Quantifies severity; helps track response to treatment.
Identifies comorbid learning or executive deficits; guides educational support.

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom count, functional impairment, and presence of comorbidities.
b: Mild: symptoms cause minor impairment, no academic failure.
Moderate: noticeable academic/social problems, may need school support.
Severe: marked dysfunction, frequent disciplinary actions, high risk of substance use.

sections.p: Neurodevelopmental disorders are multifactorial; genetics dominate, but environmental hits modify risk.
b: Genetic: polygenic risk, copy‑number variants, ADHD‑linked loci (e.g., DRD4, DAT1).
Prenatal: maternal smoking, alcohol, infections (CMV, rubella), malnutrition.
Perinatal: hypoxia, low birth weight, preterm birth.
Post‑natal: early childhood adversity, lead exposure, untreated sleep apnea.
In low‑resource settings: perinatal infections (malaria, HIV), severe anemia, chronic otitis media.

sections.p: Children show age‑inappropriate restlessness, difficulty sustaining attention, impulsive actions, and may argue or defy authority.
b: Inattention: careless mistakes, forgetfulness, losing items.
Hyperactivity: fidgeting, running/climbing excessively.
Impulsivity: blurting answers, interrupting.
ODD: frequent temper loss, blaming others.
CD: aggression toward people/animals, property destruction.

sections.p: No single lab test diagnoses ADHD; investigations aim to rule out mimics and identify comorbidities.

t.b: Excludes anemia or infection that can mimic fatigue and inattention; low hemoglobin suggests treatable anemia.
Detects hypothyroidism, which can cause concentration problems; normal TSH rules it out.
Elevated lead can cause attention deficits; chelation considered if >10 µg/dL.
Chronic HIV may affect cognition; a positive result redirects care to antiretroviral therapy.
Identifies structural lesions; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam and refer when possible.

sections.p: Certain features demand urgent evaluation or signal poor prognosis.
b: Severe aggression with weapons or self‑harm.
Sudden loss of previously acquired skills.
Unexplained weight loss, seizures, or visual changes.
Co‑existing psychosis or mood disorder.

sections.p: A stepped approach: psychoeducation, behavioural interventions, then medication when impairment remains moderate‑severe.
b: Parent‑training programmes (e.g., Triple P) improve compliance.
School‑based behavioural plans (token systems, clear expectations).
Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine) – first‑line for core ADHD symptoms; avoid in uncontrolled hypertension or severe anxiety.
Non‑stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) – useful when stimulants fail or cause tics.
For ODD/CD: structured therapy (CBT, anger‑management), family therapy; antipsychotics only for severe aggression.

sections.p: Regular review monitors symptom control, side effects, academic progress and emerging comorbidities.
b: Visit every 3‑6 months initially, then annually if stable.
Screen for substance use, mood disorders, and school dropout.
Promote sleep hygiene, balanced diet, and physical activity to reduce symptom burden.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ADHD or disruptive behaviour.
b: Learning disorders – primary academic deficits without attention problems.
Anxiety/depression – may cause inattention but with pervasive low mood.
Thyroid disease or anemia – reversible metabolic causes.
Autism spectrum disorder – social communication deficits dominate.

sections.p: Laboratory or behavioural findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal CBC does not exclude iron deficiency if ferritin not measured.
Negative lead screen may miss recent exposure; repeat if risk persists.
Rating scales can be biased by cultural expectations; corroborate with observation.

faq.a: No; it is a chronic condition, but symptoms can be well‑controlled with therapy and medication.
They increase dopamine and norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex, rapidly improving attention and impulse control.
Many improve with age, but a substantial proportion retain symptoms into adulthood.

exam: List the DSM‑5 criteria for ADHD and explain how you would confirm cross‑setting impairment.
Describe the first‑line pharmacologic treatment for ADHD, including contraindications.
Identify three red‑flag features that require urgent referral in a child with disruptive behaviour.
